title: Oholah and Oholibah: Two Sisters, One Unfaithfulness
summary: Ezekiel tells the history of Israel's two kingdoms as the story of two sisters married to the LORD: Oholah, who is Samaria, and Oholibah, who is Jerusalem. Both are unfaithful from their youth in Egypt, chasing Assyria, Babylon, and Egypt as lovers; Samaria is destroyed by the lovers she pursued, and Jerusalem, having learned nothing, will drink her sister's cup. The chapter uses deliberately shocking sexual language to expose political alliances and idolatry as betrayal of God.
story: This is the second of Ezekiel's long allegories of Israel as an unfaithful wife. Chapter 16 told the story of one woman, Jerusalem, from abandoned infant to queen to adulteress, and ended with a promise of restoration. Chapter 23 adds the northern kingdom and changes the focus. Here the lovers are named nations and the sin is chiefly political: seeking security from empires instead of from God, and taking their gods along with their protection. The chapter comes near the end of Ezekiel's warnings before the siege, and it offers no restoration at its close. The next chapter announces that the siege of Jerusalem has begun.
historical:
The chapter compresses about three centuries of foreign policy. The northern kingdom, with its capital at Samaria, repeatedly bought Assyrian favor. King Jehu appears on the Black Obelisk of the Assyrian king Shalmaneser III (about 841 BC) bowing and bringing tribute, and King Menahem paid a heavy tribute to Tiglath-pileser III, called Pul in 2 Kings 15:19-20. When the north later rebelled and turned to Egypt, Assyria besieged Samaria, and the city fell in 722 BC (2 Kings 17:3-6). Ezekiel sees that as the lovers turning on the one who courted them.

Judah followed the same road. King Ahaz appealed to Tiglath-pileser for help and sent him silver and gold from the temple (2 Kings 16:7-9). Hezekiah welcomed envoys from the Babylonian king Merodach-baladan and showed them his treasuries (2 Kings 20:12-19). In Ezekiel's own lifetime, Judah's last kings swung between Babylon and Egypt, Jehoiakim and then Zedekiah rebelling against Nebuchadnezzar in hope of Egyptian support. The people named in verse 23 alongside the Babylonians are obscure; Pekod is usually identified with an Aramean tribe in southern Babylonia known from Assyrian texts, while Shoa and Koa are less certain.
cultural:
Treaties in the ancient Near East were religious as well as political. A vassal swore oaths in the names of the overlord's gods and often honored those gods, which is why the chapter can move so easily from lusting after the Assyrians to defiling herself with their idols (verse 7). To the prophets, running to an empire for protection meant trusting another power in place of the LORD, and the covenant between God and Israel was often pictured as a marriage (Hosea 1 to 3; Jeremiah 2:2; 3:6-11). Adultery was the natural image for breaking it. Jeremiah 3 had already told the story of two unfaithful sisters, Israel and Judah.

The names are symbolic. Both come from the Hebrew word ohel, tent. Oholah is usually explained as her tent and Oholibah as my tent is in her, which many readers take as a contrast between the north's own shrines and the LORD's sanctuary in Jerusalem, though the explanation is not certain. The splendid Assyrian horsemen in blue and the Babylonian officers painted in vermilion on walls reflect the real impression these empires made; their palaces were decorated with reliefs and colored images of officials and soldiers. The punishments of verses 25 and 26 draw on the brutal treatment of captives in war and on ancient penalties for adultery, some of which involved disfigurement.
literary: The chapter is an extended allegory in several movements. Verses 1 to 4 introduce the sisters and name what they stand for, so that the reader is never in doubt. Verses 5 to 10 tell Oholah's story and its end. Verses 11 to 21 tell Oholibah's, stressing that she saw her sister's fate and went further. Four oracles of judgment follow (verses 22 to 27, 28 to 31, 32 to 34, and 35), including a short poem about the cup of Samaria. A final section (verses 36 to 49) sets both sisters on trial together and names the literal sins behind the metaphor: idolatry, child sacrifice, and profaning the temple and Sabbath. The language is deliberately graphic, even crude, and the Hebrew is harsher than many English translations. The shock is part of the method; Ezekiel is trying to make his hearers feel disgust at what they had come to regard as sensible statecraft.

outline.t: Two sisters, unfaithful from their youth in Egypt
Oholibah (Jerusalem) goes further: Assyria, Babylon, Egypt
Her former lovers brought against her
Handed over to those she hates
The cup of her sister Samaria
The charges named: idols, child sacrifice, a defiled sanctuary

doctrines.note: The chapter treats political dependence on empires as idolatry. Trusting a foreign power for security meant taking up its gods and abandoning the LORD, and verse 35 names the root: they forgot God and cast him behind their backs.

The marriage metaphor presents the covenant as an exclusive, personal bond. Unfaithfulness is not merely a broken rule but a betrayed relationship, and God's jealousy is the jealousy of a wronged spouse, not of a rival deity.
The lovers Israel pursued become the instruments of its punishment. Judgment here often takes the form of God handing people over to the consequences of what they chose.

words.note: Zanah, to commit prostitution or be sexually unfaithful. The prophets use it again and again for Israel's unfaithfulness to God, especially in worshiping other gods. In Ezekiel 16 and 23 the metaphor is stretched to its limit.

Agav, to lust after or desire intensely. It is used in the Old Testament almost only in this chapter (and once in Jeremiah 4:30), and it portrays the sisters' pursuit of foreign powers as infatuation, a desire that blinds them to where it leads.
Kos, cup. In the prophets the cup often stands for God's judgment, a portion that must be drunk to the bottom (Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15). Jerusalem will drink the same cup Samaria drank.
Oholah, the name given to Samaria, built on the word for tent. Its partner name Oholibah, given to Jerusalem, uses the same root. The pairing insists that the sisters are one family with one history.

christ: The chapter's image of the cup of judgment is taken up in the Gospels. In Gethsemane Jesus prays that the cup might pass from him, yet not as he wills but as the Father wills (Matthew 26:39), and Christians have long understood that cup as the judgment the prophets described, drunk by the one who had not been unfaithful. The marriage metaphor itself also runs through the New Testament, but reversed in hope: Paul describes the church as a bride presented to Christ (2 Corinthians 11:2; Ephesians 5:25-27), and Revelation ends with the bride made ready for the Lamb (Revelation 19:7-8). Ezekiel 23 offers no such hope within its own verses; the link is the wider prophetic story, including Ezekiel 16:60-63 and Hosea 2, in which God promises to renew the covenant with the people who broke it.

hard.q: How should a reader handle this chapter's graphic sexual imagery and its violence against a woman's body?
hard.a:
Many readers find this chapter, along with chapter 16, among the most disturbing in the Bible, and the difficulty should be admitted plainly. It portrays a nation as a woman, describes her sexuality in explicit terms, and depicts her stripping, mutilation, and death as God's judgment. Modern readers ask whether such language degrades women, and some interpreters, including feminist scholars, have argued that it sexualizes violence and has been used to excuse abuse.

Several responses are offered by those who take the text seriously as Scripture. First, the woman is a metaphor for a city and a nation, and the original audience was the male elders and leaders of Israel (see 20:1). The shock was aimed at men who were being told that their proud foreign policy was the conduct of a faithless wife, an insult in their honor culture. Second, the violence described is what conquering armies actually did to captured cities, their women, and their children; the prophet is describing the coming catastrophe in the terms of its brutal reality, not prescribing how anyone should treat a woman. Third, the metaphor is meant to expose the depth of betrayal, and its excess is part of the rhetoric of alarm. Most interpreters across traditions agree on an important boundary: the chapter is a word of judgment against a nation's covenant unfaithfulness, not a model for human marriage, and it can never be used to justify the humiliation or abuse of any woman. Readers may also set it within Ezekiel's whole book, which goes on to promise cleansing, a new heart, and a restored people.

If this chapter stirs memories of abuse, or if you are being hurt or threatened by a partner, that is not God's will for you, and help is available. In the United States you can call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 1-800-799-7233; elsewhere, contact local emergency services or a domestic violence service, and consider speaking with a trusted pastor or counselor.

questions: Judah sought security from Assyria, Babylon, and Egypt rather than from God. Where do people today look for the kind of safety only God can give?
Oholibah saw what happened to her sister and did worse. Why is it so hard to learn from the failures we have watched in others?
How does thinking of sin as betrayal of a relationship, rather than only the breaking of a rule, change the way you understand it?
